_readme: The activity registry. Adding an activity should mean adding a block here
and writing the content — nothing else.
Previously the list lived in three places (a CHECK constraint in the database,
a JS array, and label maps in the admin dashboard) and had already drifted.
This is the single source for anything user-facing.
slug      Must match activity_runs.activity and the Quiz.init() argument.
purpose   Drives the filter buttons on the hub. One of the keys in
`purposes` below. Pick the one the person would pick, not the
one that is technically most accurate.
tags      Shown on the card. Short, human, max ~3 or the card gets noisy.
keywords  NOT shown. Searched. This is where you put the words people
actually type — 'don't know what to do', 'stuck', 'career change'
— including phrasings you would never print on a card.
minutes   Honest estimate. People decide on this more than anything else.
status    live | soon | retired. Only `live` is startable; `soon` renders
greyed with no link; `retired` is hidden entirely.
tier      free | paid. Cosmetic today (a lock badge). Real gating has to
happen server-side — see DYNAMIC-ACTIVITIES.md.
sort      Ascending. Leave gaps of 10 so you can insert without renumbering.
description  Two or three sentences. Shown when somebody opens a locked
card, and it is the only pitch that activity gets to make while
they cannot start it. Say what happens in it, not why it matters.
provides  Fact keys this activity is a good way to establish. EDITORIAL,
not mechanical: every quiz that scores axes technically feeds
top_category, so listing all of them would name six activities
and help nobody. List the ones whose job it actually is.
Used to turn a `requires` into 'complete X, Y or Z to unlock'.
requires  OPTIONAL. Natural prerequisites only: an activity that CANNOT
work without prior data, never one locked to manufacture
progression. {facts:[...], runs:n, distinctActivities:n, because}.
`because` is mandatory and is shown on the locked card.
Gating is motivational, not security: it resolves client-side.
See ACTIVITY-SPEC.md.

purposes.label: Explore options
purposes.blurb: Work out what's out there and what fits

purposes.label: Narrow it down
purposes.blurb: Choose between things you're weighing up

purposes.label: Get ready to apply
purposes.blurb: Turn a direction into something you can send

purposes.label: Check in
purposes.blurb: Revisit where you are as things change

activities.name: Your Why
activities.tagline: The reason underneath all of it, in your own words.
activities.description: Two minutes and mostly your own words. Why you're looking at all, who it's for, and how long it's been true. What you write goes to the top of your profile, so it's there on the week you can't remember why you started.

activities.name: The Story
activities.tagline: Seven chapters of a life eighteen months from now.
activities.description: Seven short chapters set eighteen months from now. You pick what your day looks like, what you'd stay late for, what you'd want to be able to point at. At the end it reads back the shape of the answers and names the kinds of work that fit it.
keywords: what should i do with my life

activities.name: 168 Hours
activities.description: There are 168 hours in a week and everybody gets the same number. You divide yours up, per day for the things you know per day and per week for the rest, and see what's left over once work, getting there and keeping life running have taken their share.

activities.name: Proof
activities.tagline: Three things you're good at, with the evidence.
activities.description: Not what appeals to you. What you've already done. You write down moments where something worked out and you were the reason, tag what the skill was, and leave with a sentence you can paste straight into an application.
keywords: nothing to put on a cv

activities.name: A Day In The Life
activities.tagline: Six moments in a day you'd actually want.
activities.description: Six moments from a single working day. Who's around, what the pressure feels like, what you do when it goes wrong. It's the same nine categories as The Story, reached from the texture of the day instead of the shape of the year.

activities.name: The Floor
activities.tagline: The number you need, not the number you want.
activities.description: You build up what your month costs, line by line, and get the number a job has to clear before anything else about it matters. Then you guess what the work pays and see the published figure next to your guess.
keywords: can i afford to change careers

activities.name: Spend Your 100
activities.tagline: What you'd really pay for in a job.
activities.description: A hundred points and six things you might want from a job. You can't have all of them, so you spend. What's left tells you which of them you'd defend and which you were only saying.

activities.name: Fixed or Assumed
activities.tagline: Which of your reasons are actually true.
activities.description: Ten cards, each one a reason a change isn't possible. You sort them into what's genuinely fixed and what you've never actually checked. Then you pick the one you'd least like to be wrong about.

activities.name: Career ABCs
activities.tagline: Build the resume, the cover letter and the interview.
activities.description: The long one. Turns what you've got into a resume, a cover letter and answers to the questions you'll be asked, one section at a time, with everything saved as you go.

activities.name: What Might Trip You Up
activities.tagline: Find the thing most likely to knock this off course, while you can still plan for it.
activities.description: A few minutes imagining that the change didn't work out, so you can spot what would most likely get in the way while there's still time to do something about it. It's a trick people who plan difficult things for a living use all the time, and it works because we're all better at explaining a problem that has already happened than at seeing one coming. Nothing you pick is a prediction, and none of it is shared.

requires.because: It walks through how a move into one particular field might go wrong, so it needs to know which field you're weighing up.

activities.name: Three Doors
activities.tagline: Every realistic route in, side by side.
activities.description: Every realistic way into the field your answers point to, side by side, with how long each takes, what it costs and what you need to get in. You mark the ones you could start within a year and the ones you couldn't.

requires.because: It compares the ways into one specific field — degree, apprenticeship, certificate, sideways move — so it needs to know which field.

activities.name: Two Conversations
activities.tagline: Who to talk to, and the message already written.
activities.description: Fifteen minutes with somebody who does the work will tell you more than anything else here. This works out who that person is, writes the message for you, and gives you the one question worth asking.

requires.because: It writes you a message to someone doing the work you're considering — which needs to know what that work is.

activities.name: Still True?
activities.tagline: What's changed since last time, and whether it still holds.
activities.description: Everything you've told us, in your words, with the date on it. You go through and say what still holds. Things you mark as changed are recorded as a change rather than quietly overwritten, and your confidence score can go down as a result.

requires.because: It works by comparing what you said before against what's true now, so it needs at least two activities to compare.
